children: The European Union is putting a ceiling on how much cash can change hands in a single deal. Starting July 10, 2027, businesses across all member states will be barred from accepting cash payments above €10,000.
There's a second layer too. Cash transactions over €3,000 will require identity verification, so the anonymous envelope of banknotes is about to get a lot more paperwork attached.

The rule comes from Regulation (EU) 2024/1624, part of the bloc's broader push against money laundering and terrorist financing. For anyone who pays for cars, jewelry or renovations in physical notes, the countdown has started.
The core mechanic is simple. No business or service provider in the EU may take a cash payment for goods or services that exceeds €10,000.
The cap covers more than single handovers. Linked payments are also caught, so splitting a €15,000 purchase into two neat €7,500 installments won't get around it.

Below the €10,000 line, cash is still permitted, but it gets less private past a certain point. For cash transactions over €3,000, the businesses involved will need to carry out customer due diligence, which means identity checks.
Not every cash exchange is in scope. Private transactions between non-professional individuals are exempt from the restrictions.

Payments and deposits made at banks and electronic money issuers are also exempt. Those institutions already operate under their own identification and reporting duties, so the new cap doesn't apply there.
The €10,000 figure works as a floor for strictness rather than a ceiling. Member states keep the power to impose tighter national limits than the EU-wide cap.
Spain is a useful example. Its existing €1,000 limit stays in force, which means Spanish shoppers won't suddenly gain new room to pay in cash once the EU rule arrives.
The regulation was formally adopted in May 2024 and published in the Official Journal in June 2024, leaving a multi-year transition window before the July 2027 start date.
Recent discussion around the rule has mostly reaffirmed the July 2027 deadline. There have been no indications of delays or changes to the original plan.

Until now, member states have handled cash transactions in very different ways, creating a patchwork where the rules depend heavily on which border you happen to be standing behind. A uniform cap is meant to close the gaps that let large cash sums slide through the least restrictive jurisdiction.
The most immediate impact lands on cash-heavy sectors. Dealers in high-value goods, such as vehicles, luxury items or art, may need to rethink how they take payment from customers who prefer notes.
For these businesses, the compliance burden is twofold. They need systems to refuse cash above €10,000, and they need processes to verify identity for cash deals over €3,000.
Linked payment rules add another wrinkle. Sellers will have to watch for customers breaking a big purchase into smaller pieces, which pushes some monitoring responsibility onto merchants themselves.
For consumers, the change is narrower than the headline figure might suggest. Most everyday purchases fall well under €3,000, and private sales between individuals remain untouched.

The national flexibility built into the rule also matters for cross-border shoppers. A buyer moving between EU countries will face the €10,000 cap everywhere, but may hit much lower limits in places like Spain.

title: EU will ban cash payments over €10,000 starting July 2027
